rows.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع
rows.claim: They read barq with an open rāʾ; the other readers use a kasra.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر ونافع: برق بفتح الراء، وقرأ الباقون بكسرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two vowelings may have the same meaning; alternatively, kasra derives from passing beyond, while fatḥ refers to a flash or a startled stare at terror.
rows.anchor: قيل: هما بمعنى، وقيل: من كسر فهو من برق يبرق: إذا جاوز

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: He reads khusifa as passive, connecting it to the following verb, “and the sun and moon were gathered.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة: خسف بضم الخاء وكسر السين على ما لم يسم فاعله قال: لقوله: وجمع

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: His codex wording says that the sun and moon were gathered together between them.
rows.anchor: وفي حرف ابن مسعود: (جمع بين الشمس والقمر)

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم وأبو عبيدة
rows.claim: They prefer al-mafar with fatḥ because it is a verbal noun; Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan read it with kasra, which al-Kisāʾī calls a dialectal variant and another grammarian takes as a place of refuge.
rows.anchor: المفر بفتح الفاء، واختاره أبو حاتم وأبو عبيدة قالا: لأنه مصدر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: They read al-mafar with kasra; al-Kisāʾī calls both forms dialects, while another grammarian assigns kasra the sense of a place of refuge.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس والحسن بكسر الفاء قال الكسائي: هما لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barq is a brief flash of light; barq al-baṣar describes an eye flashing, and al-bāriqa names swords shining when drawn.
rows.anchor: البرق: لمعان بالشعاع الذي لا يلبث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wizr means a refuge such as a fortress; wazīr is related as a helper to whom one turns, and a wall is strengthened with a foundation.
rows.anchor: والوزر: ملجأ من حصن أو غيره، ومنه: الوزير: المعين الذي يلجأ إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mustaqarr is a place of settlement, like al-maʾwā and al-mathwā, and may be temporary or everlasting.
rows.anchor: والمستقر: موضع القرار، ونظيره: المأوى والمثوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-farr is the verbal noun of fleeing. A report from Surāqa calls the Prophet and Abū Bakr the two fugitives of Quraysh.
rows.anchor: وفي حديث سراقة: (هذان فر قريش أفلا أرد على قريش فرها)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nabaʾ means a report of great significance.
rows.anchor: والنبأ: [الخبر] العظيم الشأن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqdīm means placing something before another, the opposite of delay; precedence can be temporal, spatial, or by rank.
rows.anchor: والتقديم: ترتيب الشيء قبل غيره، ونقيضه: التأخير، والتقديم ثلاثة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وحمزة ونافع
rows.claim: They read ʿāliyahum with a still yāʾ as an active participle from ʿalāhum, “above them.”
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر وحمزة ونافع: عاليهم بسكون الياء، وهو قراءة مجاهد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He parses the reading with fatḥ on the yāʾ as an adverbial expression meaning “above them.”
rows.anchor: وهو نصب على الظرف، كقوله: فوقهم، عن الفراء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: He rejects al-Farrāʾ's adverbial parsing and analyzes it as a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in ʿalayhim, or from the boys in raʾaytahum.
rows.anchor: وأنكر هذا القول الزجاج. وقال: إنما نصب على الحال من الضمير

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet promises that whoever recites ʿAmma yatasaʾalūn will be given a cool drink on the Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي بن كعب، عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه قال: من قرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chapter is Meccan, has forty verses, and is also called Sūrat al-Muʿṣirāt.
rows.anchor: وتسمى سورة (المعصرات)، مكية، وهي أربعون آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After al-Mursalāt ended with the Resurrection and warnings to deniers, this chapter opens with the Resurrection, proofs of God's power to restore creation, and people's conditions.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم سورة (المرسلات) بذكر القيامة، ووعيد المكذبين، افتتح هذه السورة بذكر القيامة

rows.speaker: الحسن ومالك بن دينار
rows.claim: They read both instances of “they will know” in the second person; the common reading uses third person.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ومالك بن دينار بالتاء فيهما على الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third-person reading is preferable because the preceding “they ask one another” and “about which they differ” refer back to the same people; the second person is also possible through a shift in address, but only the established public reading is recitable.
rows.anchor: والوجه الأول؛ لأنه قال: (يتساءلون) وقال: (الذي هم فيه مختلفون)

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: He reports the preposition bi- in place of min- in “from the muʿṣirāt,” analogizing a Qur'anic phrase about angels descending on the Night of Decree.
rows.anchor: وعن عكرمة: (بالمعصرات) كقوله: (تنزل الملائكة والروح فيها بإذن ربهم من كل أمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAmma contracts ʿan mā by assimilation; al-Akhfash says the alif is omitted to distinguish declarative from interrogative use, while another view compares forms such as bi-ma and fī-ma.
rows.anchor: عم أصله: (عن ما) فأدغم النون في الميم لقربها منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition joins so closely to mā that it acts like part of it, marking the tight connection.
rows.anchor: واتصالها بحرف الجر حتى صار كجزء منه لينبئ عن شدة الاتصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A question seeks information; mutual questioning is reciprocal, as each party asks the other.
rows.anchor: السؤال: طلب الإخبار بصيغة من الكلام، والتساؤل: التقابل بسؤال كل واحد من النفيسين صاحبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nabaʾ is a momentous report; nabīʾ is derived from it for those who pronounce the hamza, while those who omit it derive the word from elevation.
rows.anchor: النبأ: الخبر العظيم الشأن، ومنه النبيء على مذهب من يهمزه

rows.speaker: عاصم وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read “the sky was opened” with a light tāʾ; the other readers use the doubled form to convey repeated openings.
rows.anchor: قرأ عاصم وحمزة والكسائي: وفتحت السماء خفيفة التاء، الباقون مشددة التاء على التكثير

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: He reads labithīn without an alif; the others read lābithīn with one, and both are dialect forms.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة: لبثين بغير ألف، وهي قراءة علقمة، والباقون: لابثين بألف وهما لغتان

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي وحفص عن عاصم
rows.claim: They read ghassāqan with a doubled sīn; the others use a light sīn, and both are dialect forms.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة، والكسائي، وحفص عن عاصم: غساقا بتشديد السين، الباقون بالتخفيف، وهما لغتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-faṣl is the decisive judgment and originally means cutting; the Day is named for God's judgment between creatures, like the Day of Conquest.
rows.anchor: الفصل: فصل الحكم، وأصله: القطع، وسميت القيامة يوم الفصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mīqāt is a set time for an event; the pattern names the thing by which an event is timed, like mīʿād from a promise and mīzān from weighing.
rows.anchor: والميقات: الوقت المضروب لحدوث أمر، وأصله الوقت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fawj means a group of people, with afwāj as its plural.
rows.anchor: والفوج: الجماعة من الناس، والجمع: أفواج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mirage is a white appearance at sunrise or midday that looks like water to an observer; at the hottest hour it is called ālāʾ.
rows.anchor: والسراب: ما يراه الرائي عند طلوع الشمس ووقت الضحى أبيض يظنه ماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mirsād is a watchpoint equipped to observe something expected to occur.
rows.anchor: والمرصاد: مفعال من الرصد المعد لأثر على ارتقاب الوقوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāghī, ʿātī, and ʿādī all describe someone who exceeds the limit in disobedience.
rows.anchor: والطاغي والعاتي والعادي سواء، وهو من جاوز الحد في العصيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥqāb means many stretches of time; its singular is variously given as ḥuqb or ḥuqb, and a ḥuqba is one such span. An unnamed poet uses it for a long period.
rows.anchor: والأحقاب: الأزمان الكثيرة، واحدها: حقب، ومنه: (أو أمضي حقبا)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wifāq means corresponding to a measure; punishment corresponds to the measure of deeds merited.
rows.anchor: والوفاق: الجاري على مقدار، فالجزاء وفاق؛ لأنه جار على مقدار الأعمال

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He has “at that time” in place of “after that”; the author suggests this may be an explanatory gloss rather than a reading.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد عند ذلك دحاها ولعله قاله تفسيرا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He reads al-arḍ in the nominative as a new subject; the common reading puts it in the accusative, with “He spread the earth” understood.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والأرض بالرفع على الابتداء

rows.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: He reads al-jibāl in the nominative as a new sentence; the common reading is accusative, with “He fixed the mountains” understood.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمرو بن عبيد بالرفع على الاستئناف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samk means height or an elevated structure; the heavens are called al-masmūkāt for their height, and ʿAlī's prayer and al-Farazdaq's line illustrate the term.
rows.anchor: ومنه حديث علي: يا بارئ السبع المسموكات، ويقال: سنام سامك

rows.speaker: الفرزدق
rows.claim: His line “the One who raised the sky built for us a house” uses samaka for raising or making high.
rows.anchor: وقال الفرزدق: إن الذي سمك السماء بنى لنا ... بيتا دعائمه أعز وأطول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opposite of height is depth; samk is construction above, while depth is below.
rows.anchor: ونقيض السمك: العمق، والسمك: البناء في العلو، والعمق في السفل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taswiya means making one thing match another in its form and meaning.
rows.anchor: والتسوية: جعل أحد الشيئين على مقدار الآخر في نفسه ومعناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghaṭsh means darkness: the night darkens, and God made it dark.
rows.anchor: والغطش: الظلمة، وغطش الليل: أظلم، وأغطشه الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daḥw means spreading out; the verb has both forms daḥā yadḥū and daḥā yadḥī, like other verbs with parallel endings.
rows.anchor: والدحو: البسط، دحا دحوا، يدحو ويدحى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marʿā is vegetation fit for grazing, named from the livestock grazing on and eating it.
rows.anchor: والمرعى: النبات الذي يصلح لرعي الماشية، وهي ترعاه بأن تأكله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Irsāʾ means securing something with weight; a ship is said to be anchored when its weight holds it in place.
rows.anchor: والإرساء: الإثبات بالثقل، رست السفينة: ثبتت بثقلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāmma means an immense, overwhelming occurrence; it can describe what rises above and overcomes everything, or a calamity that cannot be repelled. The Resurrection is named for overpowering all else.
rows.anchor: الطامة: الغاشية الغليظة، التي توفي كل شيء بالغلظ والكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings identify it as the second blast or the time when the people of Paradise and Hell are led to their destinations.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الطامة النفخة الثانية، عن الحسن، وقيل: حين يساق أهل الجنة إلى الجنة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He interprets al-ṭāmma as the second blast.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الطامة النفخة الثانية، عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes al-ṭāmma as the time when the people of Paradise are led to Paradise and the people of Hell to Hell.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حين يساق أهل الجنة إلى الجنة، وأهل النار إلى النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When people read their records, they recall their worldly good and evil and recognize that no deed, small or great, was lost.
rows.anchor: يعني: يذكر عند قراءة الكتب ما عمل في الدنيا من خير أو شر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fire is revealed for people to see; alternatively, it appears before them and they know it is their destination.
rows.anchor: أي: ظهرت النار لمن رآها، وقيل: يراها بارزة، ويعلم أنها مقره

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر والعباس عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: They read mundhir with tanwīn; the other readers omit the tanwīn.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر والعباس عن أبي عمرو: منذر بالتنوين، الباقون بغير التنوين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Choosing worldly life over the Hereafter is blameworthy, whereas choosing the Hereafter is praiseworthy.
rows.anchor: فمن آثر الدنيا على الآخرة فهو مذموم، ومن آثر الآخرة فهو ممدوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ayyān means “when” and is commonly used to ask about time, as ayn asks about place.
rows.anchor: و(أيان) معناه: متى، وكثر استعماله في السؤال عن الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marsā can mean the ship's becoming fixed, the source noun for anchoring, or the time of anchoring.
rows.anchor: والمرسى: قيامها ثابتة، ويحتمل أن يكون المراد به المرسى المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muntahā is the place at which something reaches its end.
rows.anchor: والمنتهى: موضع بلوغ الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creation of the heavens, earth, mountains, light, and darkness proves resurrection: if God can preserve created substances, He can restore and revive them after their destruction.
rows.anchor: الآيات تدل على صحة البعث بما بين من خلق السماء، والأرض والجبال، والنور والظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses also demonstrate the Resurrection's tremendous condition and many terrors.
rows.anchor: وتدل على عظيم حال القيامة، وكثرة أهوالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses distinguish obedience from rebellion: Paradise is attained through obedience and Hell deserved for sins, against the determinists' claim.
rows.anchor: تبيين حال المطيع من حال العاصي، وأن الجنة تنال بالطاعة، والنار تستحق بالمعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Preferring worldly life and working for it while heedless of the Hereafter is blameworthy.
rows.anchor: أن من آثر الدنيا وعمل لها غافلا عن الآخرة فقد ارتكب أمرا قبيحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden is earned by preferring obedience and avoiding sins; the command to restrain the self from desire includes both.
rows.anchor: أن الجنة تنال بإيثار الطاعة، والاجتناب عن المعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The time of the Resurrection is known only to God.
rows.anchor: ومنها: أن وقت القيامة لا يعلمه غير الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People will regard worldly life as brief when they witness the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: ومنها: أنهم يستقلون الدنيا عند معاينته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Obedience and sin are acts of human beings, as the verses attribute rebellion and fear to them; this refutes determinism.
rows.anchor: أن الطاعة والمعصية فعل العبد؛ لذلك قال: (فأما من طغى)، وقال: (وأما من خاف مقام ربه) فيبطل الجبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water poured down is rain from clouds, though the wording can encompass other waters because God brings them forth.
rows.anchor: أي: أنزلنا الغيث من السحاب إنزالا، يحتمل أنه يريد المطر، ويحتمل سائر المياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God splits the earth so the fragile plant can root and send up its shoot.
rows.anchor: ثم شققنا الأرض شقا ليخرج النبات مع ضعفه، فيرسخ عرقه ويظهر فرعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that God directly separates the earth's parts and brings the crop out without an intermediary cause.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أنه تعالى يشققها بأن يفرق بين أجزائها، ويخرج الزرع منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other explanation is that forces in the plant push earth-parts outward, so the earth is split through the plant as a cause.
rows.anchor: وثانيها: أنه يجعل في أجزاء النبات اعتمادات تخرج أجزاء الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first account makes the split God's act without a cause; the second makes it an act through a cause.
rows.anchor: فعلى الوجه الأول هو فعله بغير سبب، وعلى الثاني فعله بسبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥabb means the general class of grains that people store and eat as staples.
rows.anchor: حبا أراد جنس الحبوب التي تدخر وتقتات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Olives are singled out for the great benefit of their oil and other uses.
rows.anchor: وزيتونا الذي منه الزيت، وخصه بالذكر لعظم النفع به وما يتخذ منه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك والفراء وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: They explain qadban as fresh, tender fodder.
rows.anchor: قيل: الرطبة، عن ابن عباس، والضحاك، والفراء، وأبي مسلم

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو علي
rows.claim: They explain qadban as fodder for livestock.
rows.anchor: وقيل: القضب: العلف، عن الحسن، وأبي علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghalban describes enclosed orchards containing large, thick, varied trees.
rows.anchor: حدائق غلبا أي: بساتين محوطة تشتمل على أشجار عظام غلاظ مختلفة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He explains ghalban as trees growing intertwined or densely together.
rows.anchor: وقيل: غلبا ملتفة، عن مجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He explains ghalban as tall trees.
rows.anchor: وقيل: طوالا، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He explains ghalban as noble or fine palms.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الغلب: النخل الكرام، عن قتادة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: He explains ghalban as trees with massive trunks and necks.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عظام الجذوع والرقاب، عن ابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says fruit is not included in what preceded; another says some fruits are named first for their merit, followed by the class as a whole.
rows.anchor: قيل: ليس ذلك بفاكهة، وقيل: ذكر بعضها لفضله، ثم ذكر جملتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation treats abban as pasture for livestock, corresponding to fruit for people.
rows.anchor: وأبا قيل: المرعى للأنعام كالفاكهة للناس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وقتادة ومجاهد
rows.claim: They explain abban as herbage or pasture.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الحشيش والمرعى، عن ابن عباس، والحسن، وقتادة، ومجاهد

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: He explains abban as vegetation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الأب: النبات، عن أبي رزين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He is also reported to explain abban as fresh fruits or as figs.
rows.anchor: وقيل الثمار الرطبة، عن ابن عباس. وقيل: هو التين، عن الضحاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Matāʿ means a benefit for people and their livestock.
rows.anchor: متاعا أي: منفعة لكم ولأنعامكم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies al-ṣākhkha as the Resurrection, named for its deafening sound.
rows.anchor: فإذا جاءت الصاخة أي: القيامة، عن ابن عباس. سميت بذلك؛ لأنها تصخ الأسماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says the overwhelming blasts strike the ears with terrifying sounds.
rows.anchor: وقيل: تصك الأصوات الهائلة الآذان

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He identifies al-ṣākhkha as the second blast, at which people are revived and all creation listens.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هي النفخة الثانية التي يحيا عندها الناس، عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man flees from his wife and nearest family because he is wholly occupied with himself and cannot attend to them.
rows.anchor: فهؤلاء أقرب الناس إليه، وكان يعنى بشأنهم، فيومئذ لا يلتفت إلى واحد منهم لشغله بنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that he fears their claims against him for debts and injustices between them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: حذرا من مطالبتهم إياه لما بينه وبينهم من التبعات والمظالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that he knows they cannot help him or one another; the wording does not require literal flight, only disregard and inability to benefit each other.
rows.anchor: وليس ثم فرار، وإنما أراد لا يلتفت أحد إلى أحد، ولا يغني أحد عن أحد شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A believer may flee relatives who belong to the people of Hell and become their enemy.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يحتمل أن يكون مؤمنا وعشائره من أهل النار، فيعاديهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says people turn from family toward the only one able to remove distress, as they would turn to God if this were manifest in worldly life.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يفر عنهم لما ظهر من عجزهم وضعفهم إلى من يملك كشف الكروب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He may flee to avoid seeing the humiliation that befalls them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يفر لئلا يرى ما ينزل بهم من الهوان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation attributes the flight to distress at the magnitude of what has happened.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ضجرا لعظم ما نزل به

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He reports that Abraham flees his father, Muhammad his father, Noah his father, Abel his brother, and Lot his wife, then recited this verse.
rows.anchor: ثم تلا هذه الآية، عن الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each person has a great concern sufficient to occupy him, leaving no time for anyone else.
rows.anchor: لكل امرئ منهم يومئذ شأن يغنيه أي: أمر عظيم يكفيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The radiant faces are the people who own them, joyful and glad about the blessings announced to them.
rows.anchor: مشرقة مضيئة ضاحكة كناية عن السرور، وقيل: أراد بالوجوه أصحاب الوجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghُbra may be smoke that blackens faces, or black dust that harms and darkens them.
rows.anchor: قيل: دخان تسود به وجوههم. وقيل: غبار أسود يضر وجوههم، ويسودها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations say they put dust on their heads as suppliants, become earth, show extreme grief, are eclipsed, or bear the remaining dust of their graves.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يجوز أن يجعلوا التراب على رؤوسهم كالمستغيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qatarah is explained as darkness and blackness, smoke, or abundant dust; another view says wind drives dust and smoke into their faces from opposite sides.
rows.anchor: قترة قيل: ظلمة وسواد. وقيل: هي الدخان. وقيل: الغبار الكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those described are the disbelievers and sinners who depart from God's command.
rows.anchor: أولئك من تقدم ذكرهم هم الكفرة الفجرة الخارجون عن أمر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage includes an obligation to consider the proofs.
rows.anchor: الآيات تتضمن أحكاما: منها: وجوب النظر في الأدلة

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: He gives two possibilities: the soul learns what it did in worldly life or what proof and excuse it has brought when questioned.
rows.anchor: عنه، ذكر الوجهين أبو مسلم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says Sūrat al-Takwīr contains twelve events, six in this life and six in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: في سورة (إذا الشمس كورت) اثنتا عشرة خصلة: ست في الدنيا، وست في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses describe changes in the heavens, earth, mountains, and stars and depict Paradise and Hell to encourage and warn.
rows.anchor: تغير أحوال السماء والأرض والجبال والنجوم، وصفة الجنة والنار ترغيبا وترهيبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person without sin must not be harmed by killing or otherwise; the rebuke for killing a buried girl shows God does not eternally punish children of polytheists or anyone for no sin or another's sin.
rows.anchor: وإذا وبخ الله من قتل الموءودة، فكيف يعاقبها أبدا سرمدا؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wild beasts will be gathered just as legally responsible people are gathered.
rows.anchor: ومنها: أن الوحوش تحشر كما يحشر المكلفون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deeds are written in records.
rows.anchor: ومنها: أن الأعمال مكتوبة في الصحف

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو والكسائي
rows.claim: They read ẓanīn with ẓāʾ, as do Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Sulamī, and ʿUrwa; the sense is “accused.”
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو والكسائي: بظنين بالظاء

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: He prefers ẓāʾ because the opponents accused the Messenger rather than finding him stingy, and Arabic uses bi- rather than ʿalā with this sense.
rows.anchor: واختاره أبو عبيدة قال: لأنهم اتهموه، ولم يبخلوه

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع وابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة ويعقوب
rows.claim: They read ḍanīn with ḍād, meaning not stingy; the reading is also in Ubayy's codex and is attributed to several early readers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون أبو جعفر ونافع وابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة ويعقوب (بضنين) بالضاد

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: He prefers ḍād: the Messenger conveys revelation and teaches people rather than withholding it.
rows.anchor: واختاره أبو حاتم، أي: ببخيل

rows.speaker: الفراء والمبرد
rows.claim: They also give ẓanīn the meaning “weak.”
rows.anchor: وقيل: ظنين: ضعيف، حكاه الفراء والمبرد

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read latarkabunna with fatḥ on the bāʾ; the reading is also attributed to ʿUmar, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, and Abū al-ʿĀliya.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وحمزة والكسائي: لتركبن طبقا بفتح الباء

rows.speaker: عمر وابن مسعود وابن عباس وأبو العالية
rows.claim: This reading may address Muḥammad, who ascends heaven after heaven and rank after rank.
rows.anchor: ومعناه: لتركبن يا محمد سماء بعد سماء، ودرجة بعد درجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that the sky changes color, is folded, or is split in successive stages.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد به السماء تتغير لونا بعد لون، تصير تارة كالدهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address may instead be to humanity or to any hearer.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لتركبن أيها الإنسان أو أيها السامع

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: He prefers the reading with ḍamma because the meaning fits the people better than the Prophet, who had been mentioned before the address turns to them.
rows.anchor: واختاره أبو عبيد؛ لأن المعنى بالناس أشبه منه بالنبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shafaq originally suggests delicacy or tenderness and means the faint remainder of sunlight after sunset.
rows.anchor: والشفق: البقية الضعيفة من أثر الشمس إذا غابت

rows.speaker: الخليل والأوزاعي وأبو يوسف ومحمد والشافعي ومالك
rows.claim: They define shafaq as the redness of twilight.
rows.anchor: فبعضهم يقول: الشفق: الحمرة، وهو قول الخليل، والأوزاعي، وأبي يوسف

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وثعلب
rows.claim: They and other jurists and language scholars define shafaq as the whiteness of twilight.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من يقول: البياض، وهو قول أبي حنيفة، وجماعة من الفقهاء

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He cites an Arab speaker comparing a red garment to shafaq and lines from poets using the same comparison.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: سمعت بعض العرب تقول لثوب أحمر: كأنه الشفق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wasaq means gathering; it can also name the collected load of food, measured at sixty ṣāʿs.
rows.anchor: والوسق: الجمع، وسقته وسقا: إذا جمعته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: His poetic citation uses mustawsiqāt for gathered-together things.
rows.anchor: وأنشد ابن عباس: مستوسقات لو يجدن سائقا أي: مجتمعات

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: He says wasaq can mean driving or carrying in Arabic, and means driving in this verse.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مسلم: الوسق في كلام العرب يحتمل وجهين: أحدهما: الطرد، والثاني: الحمل

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet promises forgiveness to one who recites al-Fajr and a light on the Resurrection Day to one who recites it daily.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي بن كعب، عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: من قرأ سورة (الفجر) غفر له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the previous chapter said that all creatures return to God and He judges them, this chapter emphasizes that He watches over them, warning and encouraging them.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم السورة المتقدمة بأن مصير الخلق إليه وحسابهم عليه، افتتح هذه السورة بتأكيد ذلك بالقسم

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They read al-watr with kasra; Abū ʿUbayd prefers it as the more common form, while the others read fatḥ, the Hijazi dialect preferred by Abū Ḥātim.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة والكسائي: والوتر بكسر الواو، وهي قراءة الأعمش ويحيى بن وثاب

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: He prefers kasra for al-watr because it is more frequent and widespread in speech.
rows.anchor: واختاره أبو عبيد، قال: لأنه أكثر في الكلام، وأفشى

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: He prefers fatḥ, which he identifies as the Hijazi dialect; both forms are dialects.
rows.anchor: وهي لغة الحجاز، واختارها أبو حاتم، وهما لغتان

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع وأبو عمرو وقتيبة عن الكسائي
rows.claim: They retain the yāʾ in yasrī when linking, but omit it when stopping.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر ونافع وأبو عمرو وقتيبة عن الكسائي: يسري بإثبات الياء في الوصل وحذفها في الوقف

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ويعقوب
rows.claim: They retain the yāʾ in yasrī both when linking and when stopping.
rows.anchor: وقرأ. ابن كثير ويعقوب بإثباتها في الوصل والوقف

rows.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر والكسائي وحمزة
rows.claim: They omit the yāʾ in both connected and paused reading; Abū ʿUbayd reports that al-Kisāʾī later settled on this omission.
rows.anchor: قرأ عاصم. وابن عامر والكسائي وحمزة بحذف الياء في الوصل والوقف

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: He prefers retaining the yāʾ when linking and omitting it at pause, while omission is also explained by the written form, ease, and rhyme.
rows.anchor: الياء في الوصل وحذفها في الوقف، وهو اختيار أبي حاتم

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: He says deleting the yāʾ is irregular because the word is a verb; deletion is expected in nouns, not verbs.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: حذفت على غير القياس، وكان الأصل ألا تحذف

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: He explains deletion of the yāʾ as matching the verse endings.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل: أسقطت الياء وفاقا لرؤوس الآي

rows.speaker: المؤرج
rows.claim: He reports al-Akhfash's explanation that night is not itself the traveler; it is the time in which people travel.
rows.anchor: ثم سألته، فقال: الليل لا يسري، وإنما يسرى فيه

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet promises safety from God's anger on the Resurrection Day to whoever recites Sūrat al-Balad.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي بن كعب، عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: من قرأ سورة (البلد) أعطاه الله الأمن من غضبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After al-Fajr's promise, warning, and account of the two groups, this chapter explains how success is attained and reinforces its oath.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم سورة (الفجر) بالوعد والوعيد وذكر العبد وحال الفريقين، بين في هذه السورة ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: He reads lubadan with a doubled bāʾ as a plural, like rākiʿ and rukkaʿ.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر وحده: لبدا مشددة الباء على الجمع

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He reads lubadan with ḍamma on both lām and bāʾ, like amrun nukur or rijāl junub.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مجاهد بضم اللام والباء، كقولك: أمر نكر، ورجال جنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common form, with ḍamma on lām and fatḥ on bāʾ, may be a plural of lubda or a singular form like qaym.
rows.anchor: والقراء كلهم على ضم اللام وفتح الباء مخففة، وفيه وجهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥill means the opposite of forbidden; ḥalāl and ḥill have the same sense.
rows.anchor: الحل: ضد الحرام، والحلال والحل سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kabad means hardship or severity; the word also describes thickened milk and the organ liver, and is a verbal noun for pain in the liver.
rows.anchor: والكبد: شدة الأمر، ومنه: تكبد اللبن: إذا غلظ واشتد

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: His verse uses fī kabad for a situation of hardship and contest.
rows.anchor: قال لبيد: يا عين هلا بكيت أربد إذ ... قمنا وقام الخصوم في كبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Labd means much or piled up, from tَلَبُّد, layering things together; Arabs say a poor person has neither support nor wealth piled up.
rows.anchor: واللبد: الكثير، وهو مأخوذ من: تلبد الشيء، إذا تراكب بعضه على بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-najdayn are the two visible, elevated routes of good and evil; najd originally means high ground.
rows.anchor: والنجدان: الطريقان، طريق الخير والشر، وأصل النجد: العلو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One occasion report says the verses through the end were revealed about Abū al-Ashaddayn of Banū Jumah, an exceptionally strong man who challenged others to remove leather pinned under his foot.
rows.anchor: قيل: نزل قوله: (لقد خلقنا الإنسان في كبد) إلى آخر الآية في رجل من بني جمح يكنى أبا الأشدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says Abū al-Ashaddayn spent much wealth opposing the Messenger, to whom the verse asks whether he thinks no one can overpower him.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن أبا الأشدين هذا أنفق مالا كثيرا في عداوة رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report identifies al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra, who said he had spent a large pile of money opposing Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نزلت الآيات في الوليد بن المغيرة، كان يقول: أهلكت مالا لبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further report identifies al-Ḥārith ibn ʿĀmir ibn Nawfal, who complained that atonements and expenses since becoming Muslim had consumed his wealth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بل نزلت في الحارث بن عامر بن نوفل بن عبد مناف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses apply generally; the wording is the basis for interpretation rather than the specific occasion.
rows.anchor: والأولى أنها على عمومها، فالمعتبر باللفظ، لا بالسبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One coherence reading asks how a person can think God does not see him when God created him and gave him eyes, a tongue, and lips.
rows.anchor: كيف يحسب أن لا يراه الله وهو الذي خلقه، وجعل له عينين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading connects the gifts of the senses to the hardship of moral responsibility: God removed the person's excuse by giving him these faculties.
rows.anchor: أنه يتصل بقوله: (لقد خلقنا الإنسان في كبد) حيث كلفناه، ولكن أزحنا علته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third reading answers the claim that no one can overpower a person: God created his eyes, tongue, and lips; the eyes see proofs and the tongue and lips speak.
rows.anchor: أنه يتصل بقوله: (أن لن يقدر عليه أحد) كيف ظن ذلك وقد خلقناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth reading uses the body's wondrous capacities as evidence against the unbeliever and says God guided him, so his unbelief is his own doing.
rows.anchor: وبدأ بالعين لعجيب خلقته في الرؤية، وباللسان لعجيب خلقته في الكلام

rows.speaker: أبو علي وجماعة
rows.claim: One view treats lā in lā uqsimu as pleonastic, so the meaning is “I swear,” as in Arab usage and the Qur'anic oath by the Lord.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر: وما ألوم البيض ألا تسخرا أي: أن تسخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes lā as a reply to a prior claim, then begins the oath: “It is not so; rather, I swear by this town.”
rows.anchor: قيل: (لا) رد لكلام سابق، ثم ابتدأ القسم

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: He gives two explanations; the first says the oath needs no further proof because the town's sanctity is already famous among Arabs and stated in scripture.
rows.anchor: فأما أبو مسلم، فذكر فيه وجهين: أحدهما: أن لا أقسم بهذا البلد وعظيم حرمته

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو عمرو والكسائي والحسن وأبو رجاء العطاردي
rows.claim: They read fakk as an active past verb with raqabatan as its object, or read aṭʿama as an active past verb “he fed.”
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو والكسائي والحسن وأبو رجاء العطاردي: فك بنصب الكاف على فعل ماض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other reading treats fakk raqabatin and iṭʿām as nouns; fakk is either linked to “he did not scale the steep path” or answers “what is the steep path?” as a nominal definition.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الباقون: فك رقبة برفع الكاف رقبة بالكسر على الإضافة أو إطعام

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو رجاء العطاردي
rows.claim: They read dhā masghaba with accusative dhā as an object of feeding; the common reading makes dhī an adjective modifying the day.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وأبو رجاء العطاردي: ذا مسغبة يعني أطعم

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وحفص عن عاصم وعبيد بن عمير وخلف بن هشام
rows.claim: They pronounce muʾṣada with hamza in both Sūrat al-Balad and Sūrat al-Humaza; other readers omit it, and Yaʿqūb reports both forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو وحفص عن عاصم وعبيد بن عمير وخلف بن هشام: مؤصدة مهموزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two forms may be dialectal; with hamza it means fully shut, and without hamza it means closed, from waṣīd for a door.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هما لغتان، وقيل بالهمز معناه: المطبقة، وبغير الهمز: المغلقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iqtiḥām is entering despite difficulty; the ʿaqaba is a steep, difficult, narrow route, likened to the demanding expense of charity.
rows.anchor: والعقبة: الطريقة التي ترتقى على صعوبة، وتحتاج منه إلى معاناة للشدة والضيق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fakk is removing a restraint, like untying a knot or freeing a neck from slavery, or releasing a pledge.
rows.anchor: والفك: فرق يزيل المنع كحل العقدة، وفك الغل والقيد

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says that reciting Sūrat al-Shams is like giving charity to everything reached by the sun and moon.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي، عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه قال: من قرأ سورة (والشمس وضحاها)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous chapter describes success through obedience and punishment for corrupting oneself; this chapter calls obedience purification instead of the previous chapter's steep path, with the same meaning.
rows.anchor: فعبر في هذه السورة عن الطاعات بالتزكية، وفى تلك السورة بالعقبة، والمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وابن عامر وعاصم
rows.claim: They pronounce the verse endings with fatḥ and tafkhīm; al-Kisāʾī uses imāla throughout, while other readers use intermediate or root-conditioned patterns.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وابن عامر وعاصم: ضحاها وتلاها وسائر أواخر الآي إلى آخر السورة بالفتح والتفخيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imāla lightens pronunciation; fatḥ is the original, while an intermediate sound both eases pronunciation and signals the original form.
rows.anchor: أما الإمالة فللتخفيف، والفتح الأصل، وما بين ذلك للتخفيف والإشعار بالأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍuḥā is the beginning of the sun's rising and of daytime; its root suggests appearing. The sacrifice term later extended to animals slaughtered after the opening period.
rows.anchor: ضحى الشمس: صدر وقت طلوعها، وكذلك وقت ضحى النهار، وهي صدر وقت كونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭaḥw means spreading out and is synonymous with daḥw; an unnamed poet uses ṭaḥā for the heart spreading toward a distant course.
rows.anchor: والطحو: البسط، طحا يطحو طحوا، ودحا يدحو دحوا بمعنى

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: He says ilhām and iltihām are equivalent; related terms mean informing, imparting, suggesting, or teaching.
rows.anchor: قال أبو مسلم: الإلهام والالتهام بمعنى، وسواء قولك: الإلهام والإلقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tazkiya means purification.
rows.anchor: والتزكية: التطهير، زكى يزكي تزكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dassa oneself is the opposite of purifying oneself: corrupt acts bury the self in loss and damage.
rows.anchor: ودس نفسه نقيض زكاها، كأنه دسها بالعمل الفاسد

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet promises that reciters of Sūrat al-Layl will receive until contentment, be protected from hardship, and have ease made easy for them.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي، عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: من قرأ سورة (والليل) أعطاه الله حتي يرضى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following the previous chapter's account of the believer and disbeliever and their outcomes, this chapter gives the same contrast again.
rows.anchor: ولما تقدم في السورة المتقدمة بيان حال المؤمن والكافر، وما فعل بهما، أتبعه بمثل ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وأبو الدرداء وعلقمة
rows.claim: They read “by the male and the female” instead of “by what created the male and the female”; the public reading is retained because Qur'an is not established by solitary reports.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن مسعود وأبي الدرداء وعلقمة: والذكر والأنثى، ولا يجوز القراءة إلا بالظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghishāʾ means covering or veiling, and tajallī means illumination and clarity.
rows.anchor: أصل الغشاء: الستر، ومنه: الغاشية والغشيان. والتجلي: الإنارة والوضوح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿy means work and earning; shattā means widely scattered or disparate, with related words denoting distance and division.
rows.anchor: والسعي: العمل والاكتساب. وشتى: متفرق على تباعد ما بين الشيئين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥusnā is the feminine form of “best” and refers to the supreme blessing because of its excellent outcome.
rows.anchor: والحسنى: تأنيث الأحسن، وهي النعمة العظمى لحسن موقعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-yusrā is the feminine form of “easier”; yusr means comfort and abundance, while taysīr means easing or lightening a matter.
rows.anchor: واليسرى: تأنيث الأيسر، كما أن الصغرى تأنيث الأصغر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿusrā is the greatest affliction, opposite of ease; taysīr's opposite makes a matter difficult.
rows.anchor: والعسرى: البلية العظمى، وهي تأنيث الأعسر، وأصله العسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taraddī can mean falling from a height or being destroyed, from al-radā.
rows.anchor: والتردي: السقوط من علو إلى سفل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā in “what created” is a masdar particle, meaning “the creation of the male and female”; al-Ḥasan instead takes it as a relative pronoun.
rows.anchor: (ما) في قوله: (وما خلق) ما المصدر، تقديره: وخلق الذكر والأنثى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage begins its account of three reported occasions for revelation with Abū Bakr; the next part continues those reports.
rows.anchor: أولها: أنها نزلت في أبي بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding occasion report identifies Abū Bakr; this segment continues the source's differing accounts and argues that the passage's point is general.
rows.anchor: وثالثها: أن النار أضيف إليهم

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: He gives three explanations of “none enters it but the most wretched”: only one matching the stated traits approaches it; the Fire is named for its majority and intended occupants; or “only” signals the most deserving, without excluding others.
rows.anchor: ذكر هذه الوجوه الثلاثة أبو مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exclusionary reading cannot mean that no sinful person enters Hell: that would contradict consensus, encourage or permit sin, and conflict with the threat against the miser and sinner.
rows.anchor: لوجب القطع على أن الفاسق لا يدخل النار، وفيه خلاف الإجماع، وإغراء بالمعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation supplies an ellipsis: “the most wretched, and whoever is like him among the sinners.”
rows.anchor: كأنه قيل: الأشقى، ومن جرى مجراه من العصاة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view says some disbelievers enter the Fire without having committed each specified act of denial, miserliness, and turning away; the author says the first explanation is best.
rows.anchor: أن من الكفار من يدخلها، وإن لم يكذب، ولم يبخل، ولم يتول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers the first of the explanations of who enters the Fire.
rows.anchor: وأحسن الوجوه هو الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yujannabuhā means that the pious person is moved far enough away from the Fire to be on the opposite side.
rows.anchor: وسيجنبها أي: يبعد منها حتى يصير في غير جانبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-atqā may mean simply the pious, or the most pious among the people of Paradise, where children, the insane, the compensated, and houris are also present.
rows.anchor: الأتقى قيل: التقي، وقيل: الأتقى من أهل الجنة، وهم المؤمنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning and promise address morally responsible people; thus children and the insane are also kept from the Fire without being included as the warned audience.
rows.anchor: قلنا: المراد به المكلفون؛ لأن الإنذار يوجه إليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving wealth to purify means giving charity and obligatory alms and cleansing oneself through acts of obedience.
rows.anchor: الذي يؤتي ماله يتزكى أي: يتصدق ويؤدي الواجب، ويتطهر بفعل الطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He has no favor owed to anyone that he is repaying; he gives for its goodness as obedience to God, not for return or compensation.
rows.anchor: وما لأحد عنده من نعمة تجزى أي: لم يتصدق ولا فعل ما فعل لجزاء ولا لعوض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking the face of his Lord means seeking God's pleasure; “face” refers to God himself, and illā means “but.”
rows.anchor: إلا ابتغاء؛ أي: طلب وجه ربه أي: رضا ربه، فذكر وجهه وأراد نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-aʿlā means the one who overpowers everything, or it may mean the most exalted.
rows.anchor: الأعلى أي: الأقدر الذي يقهر كل شيء ولا يمتنع، وقيل: الأعلى: الأجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will give him a reward that reaches his ultimate wish, leaving him satisfied and seeing no further increase; the lām emphasizes an oath-backed promise.
rows.anchor: سوف يعطيه الله من الجزاء نهاية أمنيته حتى يرضى

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet promises intercession and reward for reciting Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā, scaled to the number of every orphan and asker.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي، عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: من قرأ سورة (الضحى) جعله الله فيمن يشفع له محمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous chapter ends with God pleasing the most pious through reward; this one addresses the Prophet and promises him rank and honor at the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم سورة (والليل) بأنه يرضي الأتقى بما يعطيه من الثواب، افتتح هذه السورة خطابا للنبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading doubles the dāl in waddaʿaka, while some read it light; the senses are farewell and leaving.
rows.anchor: قراءة العامة: (ما ودعك) بالتشديد من التوديع، وعن بعضهم بالتخفيف أي: ما تركك

rows.speaker: أشهب العقيلي
rows.claim: He reads fa-awā with a short alif, meaning “he showed you mercy,” in contrast to the common long form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أشهب العقيلي: فأوى بالقصر أي: رحمك

rows.speaker: ابن السميقع
rows.claim: He reads ʿayilan with a doubled yāʾ and no alif, while the common reading has ʿāʾilan; both mean poor.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن السميقع: (عيلا) بتشديد الياء بغير ألف

rows.speaker: النخعي والشعبي
rows.claim: They read takhar with kāf instead of the common taqhar with qāf; the form also occurs in ʿAbd Allāh's codex.
rows.anchor: وعن النخعي والشعبي: (تكهر) بالكاف، وكذلك هي في مصحف عبد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic speakers sometimes interchange qāf and kāf; Muʿāwiya ibn al-Ḥakam's report that the Prophet neither rebuked nor struck him illustrates kahara.
rows.anchor: والعرب تعاقب بين القاف والكاف؛ ولذلك قال معاوية بن الحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍuḥā is the start of the day and derives from appearing in sunlight.
rows.anchor: الضحى: صدر النهار، وأصله الظهور، يقال: ضحى فلان للشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sajw is stillness; the word describes a calm eye or sea. Two poetic lines use it for a still sea and a quiet night.
rows.anchor: والسجو: السكون، سجا يسجو سجوا: إذا سكن، وطرف ساج وبحر ساج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawdīʿ means parting or farewell, but here it is a metaphor: God does not withhold His customary favor, revelation, and support, contrary to the disbelievers' claim.
rows.anchor: والتوديع: المفارقة والتبرك، ودع يودع توديعا، وهو في هذا الموضع استعارة

rows.speaker: زر بن حبيش
rows.claim: He transmits a report from the Prophet saying that whoever recites Alam nashraḥ is as if they came to him while he was distressed and relieved him.
rows.anchor: وعن زر بن حبيش عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: من قرأ (ألم نشرح لك صدرك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrat al-Sharḥ follows al-Ḍuḥā by recalling blessings like those just mentioned.
rows.anchor: واتصل بسورة (والضحى) اتصال ذكر نعمة بأمثالها

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: He reads the sīn in both occurrences of yusran with ḍamma; the common reading has sukūn.
rows.anchor: قراءة العامة: (فإن مع العسر يسرا (5) إن مع العسر يسرا)، بسكون السين

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A report in his name gives “with hardship is ease” once rather than repeating it, but the author says it cannot be relied on because it is an isolated report.
rows.anchor: وفي خبر ابن مسعود: إن مع العسر يسرا مرة واحدة غير متكررة، وهذا لا يصح الاعتماد عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sharḥ means opening and expansion; opening the chest removes distractions, and joy is described as spaciousness while grief constricts the heart.
rows.anchor: وأصل الشرح: السعة، ويعبر عن السرور بسعة القلب وشرحه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wizr means a burden; a minister carries the ruler's burden, and sins are called burdens because they weigh on their bearer.
rows.anchor: والوزر: من الثقل، ومنه: الوزير لأنه يحمل الثقل عن الملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naqḍ and hadm are near-synonyms for destroying a structure by taking it apart; anqāḍ are loads nearly breaking what bears them.
rows.anchor: والنقض والهدم من النظائر، وهو إبطال البناء بالتفريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naṣb is weariness from sustained work.
rows.anchor: والنصب: التعب، نصب ينصب: إذا تعب في عمله بالدوام فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says God opened the Prophet's heart through prophethood and knowledge, insight into religion, and ability to obey and fulfill the message.
rows.anchor: قيل: ألم نفتح ونوسع قلبك بالنبوة والعلم

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: He explains the opening as removing the Prophet's worries so that he could persevere.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ألم نشرح عنك الهموم حتى تثبت في ذلك، عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is the subtle divine help, strength, support, and promises that made the mission and harm from opponents bearable.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو الألطاف التي ترد عليه من الله من تقوية قلبه ونصرته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the Prophet was distressed by unbelief, rejection, and harm, then God expanded his heart so he no longer became upset or constricted.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كان النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - يضيق صدره بما يرى من كفرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asked about the sign of an expanded heart, the Prophet is reported to describe renouncing the deceptive world, turning to the eternal home, and preparing for death before it arrives.
rows.anchor: وعن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه سئل عن شرح الصدر وعلامته

rows.speaker: مجاهد والضحاك وابن زيد وأبو علي
rows.claim: They interpret the burden removed from the Prophet as his sin.
rows.anchor: قيل: ذنبك، عن مجاهد، والضحاك، وابن زيد، وأبي علي

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He interprets the burden as what the Prophet bore during the pre-prophetic period of ignorance.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الوزر الذي كان عليه في الجاهلية قبل النبوة، عن الحسن

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: He explains the burden as the Prophet's distress over opponents' abuse, removed when God gave him victory; the author calls this the best view.
rows.anchor: عن أبي مسلم. وهذا أحسن ما قيل فيه

rows.speaker: الحسن ومجاهد وقتادة وابن زيد
rows.claim: They explain anqaḍa as making something heavy; the expression compares the Prophet's back to a camel burdened and worn down by travel.
rows.anchor: قيل: أثقل، عن الحسن، ومجاهد، وقتادة، وابن زيد

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He explains the phrase as breaking the back so that its sound is heard; this is a metaphor and simile.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كسر ظهرك حتى سمع نقيضه؛ أي: صوته، عن الفراء

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet promises health and certainty during life and a reward after death equal to a day's fasting multiplied by the chapter's reciters.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي بن كعب، عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: من قرأ سورة (والتين)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After al-Sharḥ commands desire for God, this chapter says God created and transformed creation; therefore worship and needs should be directed to Him alone.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم سورة (ألم نشرح) بالأمر بالرغبة إليه، افتتح هذه السورة بأنه الذي خلق الخلق

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: He reads Sīnā in place of the common Sīnīn.
rows.anchor: قراءة العامة: (سينين) وعن عمر: (سينا)

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: He reads asfal al-sāfilīn with the definite article, unlike the common form without it.
rows.anchor: وقراءة العامة: (أسفل سافلين)، وعن ابن مسعود: (أسفل السافلين)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭūr means mountain; taqwīm is shaping something into proper, upright composition.
rows.anchor: الطور: الجبل. والتقويم: تصيير الشيء على ما ينبغي أن يكون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mann originally means cutting, as in al-manūn and al-maniyya because death cuts off life.
rows.anchor: والمن: أصله القطع، ومنه: المنون والمنية؛ لأنه يقطع الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn can mean recompense, reckoning, religious practice, or a customary way of life.
rows.anchor: والدين: الجزاء، والدين: الحساب، والدين: ما يدان به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may swear by the fig and olive themselves or by their Lord; they are singled out for benefits and as signs of creative power, since fig grows from wood and olive yields oil.
rows.anchor: قيل: بهذه الأشياء، وقيل: بربهما، وخصهما بالذكر لما فيهما من النفع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن ومجاهد وعطاء بن أبي رباح وقتادة وعكرمة وإبراهيم وجابر بن زيد ومقاتل والكلبي وأبو علي وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: They identify the fig as the fruit and the olive as the fruit pressed for oil; the author prefers this apparent sense absent evidence to leave it.
rows.anchor: التين الذي يؤكل، والزيتون الذي يعصر، عن ابن عباس، والحسن، ومجاهد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He also explains the fig as Noah's mosque and the olive as Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التين مسجد نوح، والزيتون بيت المقدس، عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He explains the two fruits as two mosques in Syria.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هما مسجدان بالشام، عن الضحاك

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: He identifies the fig as the mosque of the People of the Cave and the olive as the mosque of Iliya.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التين مسجد أصحاب الكهف، والزيتون مسجد إيليا، عن محمد بن كعب

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: He says the fig and olive are named with Mount Sinai because they grow on that mountain and display God's power through their contrasting qualities.
rows.anchor: ذكر الأصم أنه تعالى ذكر التين والزيتون وطور سينين؛ لأنه تعالى ينبتهما في ذلك الجبل

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: He says the fig and olive are two mountains.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هما جبلان، عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reported explanations identify them as Kufa and Syria, the places where prophets arose, or the Sacred Mosque and the Aqsa Mosque.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التين الكوفة، والزيتون الشام، وقيل: أقسم بمنابت الأنبياء

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet promises that reciting al-Qāriʿa will make a person's scale heavy on the Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي، عن النبي، صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه قال: من قرأ سورة (القارعة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿĀdiyāt ended by mentioning the Resurrection, and this chapter opens with it in a continuation of the composition.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم سورة (العاديات) بذكر القيامة، افتتح هذه السورة بذكرها

rows.speaker: حمزة ويعقوب
rows.claim: They omit the pause hāʾ in mā hiyah when linking; the others retain it, and all retain it at a stop.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة ويعقوب: (ما هيه) بحذف الهاء في الوصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarʿ is a forceful strike; al-qāriʿa is a calamity that strikes hearts with intense fear.
rows.anchor: والقارعة: البلية التي تقرع القلوب لشدة المخافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farrāsh is locusts, named for spreading out and mounting one another; mabthūth means scattered in every direction.
rows.anchor: والفراش: الجراد، وأصلهة الفرش، وسمي بذلك؛ لأنه ينفرش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mabthūth means dispersed in all directions.
rows.anchor: والمبثوث: المتفرق في الجهات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIhn means colored wool; Zuhayr's line compares wool fragments at a campsite with uncrushed desert berries.
rows.anchor: والعهن: الصوف الملون، قال زهير: كأن فتات العهن في كل منزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāḍiya has a passive sense, “pleasing,” or means “possessing satisfaction,” like other active forms used for what someone has.
rows.anchor: راضية أي: مرضية، فاعل بمعنى مفعول، على تقدير: ذات رضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two poetic examples support using an active form to mean “possessing” something, as in “possessing hardship” or “possessing dates.”
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر: كليني لهم يا أميمة ناصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hāwiya can describe rapid downward movement; Hell is named so because it plunges its inhabitants from its top to its bottom.
rows.anchor: وسميت جهنم هاوية؛ لأنها تهوي بأهلها من أعلاها إلى أسفلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Related Qur'anic expressions use hawā for moving toward something, being led astray, or falling; the word can also mean destruction.
rows.anchor: ومنه: (استهوته الشياطين) أمالته إلى ما دعته إليه، ومنه: (والمؤتفكة أهوى)

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He says Sūrat al-Takāthur is Medinan; Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda say it is Meccan.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: مدنية، وقال ابن عباس وقتادة: مكية

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet promises that the reciter will not be called to account for worldly blessings and will receive a reward like reciting a thousand verses.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي، عن النبي صلى الله عليه: من قرأ (ألهاكم التكاثر) لم يحاسبه الله بالنعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the preceding chapter warned that disbelievers' destination is Hell, this chapter explains what led them there.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم السورة بوعيد الكفار، وأن أمهم هاوية، افتتح هذه السورة ببيان ما أدى بهم إلى ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عامر والكسائي
rows.claim: They read the first tarawna with ḍamma and the second with fatḥ; ʿAlī is also reported to read this way.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن عامر والكسائي: لترون الجحيم ثم لترونها الأول بضم التاء والثاني بفتحها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilhāʾ means turning someone from serious matters toward diversion; the verb is attributed to takāthur because boasting about abundance causes distraction.
rows.anchor: وحقيقة قوله: (ألهاكم التكاثر) أي: لهيتم بالتكاثر، فأضاف الفعل إلى التكاثر اتساعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takāthur is competitive boasting in the abundance of distinctions; the tafaʿala pattern can mark reciprocity, forced pretense, or acquiring a quality.
rows.anchor: والتكاثر: التفاخر بكثرة المناقب، تكاثر القوم تكاثرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A visit is going to a place as one goes to water, without remaining there; zūr can also mean a false imitation of handwriting.
rows.anchor: والزيارة: إتيان الموضع كإتيان الماء، والمألوف على غير إقامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIlm al-yaqīn is knowledge that settles the soul after uncertainty; certainty is therefore not used as a description of God.
rows.anchor: وعلم اليقين: علم تسكن النفس إليه بعد اضطراب؛ ولذا لا يجوز اليقين في صفة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet promises that reciting Sūrat al-ʿAṣr brings patience and companionship with the people of truth on the Resurrection Day.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: من قرأ سورة (والعصر) ختم الله له بالصبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After warning about those distracted by worldly abundance, this chapter says people are in loss unless they do good and avoid disobedience.
rows.anchor: ولما ختم السورة بوعيد من ألهاه التكاثر بالدنيا، افتتح هذه السورة بأن الإنسان في خسر

rows.speaker: الأعرج
rows.claim: He reads khusr with ḍamma on the sīn; the common reading has sukūn.
rows.anchor: قراءة العامة: (لفي خسر) بسكون السين، وعن الأعرج بضمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿaṣr means time, from wringing moisture out of cloth; the image is extended to time as the span in which affairs are worked and turned.
rows.anchor: العصر: الدهر، وأصله: عصر الثوب ونحوه، وهو فتله لإخراج مائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The afternoon prayer is named for being deferred from the beginning of its time; ʿaṣāra is what is pressed from grapes, while muʿṣirāt are rain-bearing clouds.
rows.anchor: ومنه سميت صلاة العصر؛ لأنها تعصر بالتأخير عن أول وقتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iʿṣār is a column of dust that twists and rises into the sky.
rows.anchor: والإعصار: غبار ينفتل كالعمود، ويتصعد في السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khusr is the loss or destruction of one's capital.
rows.anchor: والخسر: هلاك رأس المال، وهو الخسران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣabr is restraining the self from whatever it desires to pursue.
rows.anchor: والصبر: حبس النفس عما تنازع إليه من الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wāw in al-ʿaṣr is an oath particle; the oath's answer is “humanity is surely in loss.”
rows.anchor: والعصر) مكسور لأنه قسم، والواو واو القسم، وموضع القسم قوله: (إن الإنسان لفي خسر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One report says the verse about humanity's loss was revealed concerning Abū Jahl.
rows.anchor: قيل: نزل قوله: (إن الإنسان لفي خسر) في أبي جهل بن هشام

rows.speaker: ابن علي بن عبد الله بن عباس
rows.claim: A report maps the exception to four figures: Abū Bakr believed, ʿUmar did good deeds, ʿUthmān urged truth, and ʿAlī urged patience; Ubayy ibn Kaʿb transmits it as prophetic, but the author says the exception is general.
rows.anchor: أبو بكر (وعملوا الصالحات) عمر (وتواصوا بالحق) عثمان (وتواصوا بالصبر) علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning and exception apply generally, as shown by the form of the exception.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه عام؛ ولذلك استثنى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والكلبي وأبو علي
rows.claim: They identify al-ʿaṣr as the age or time, whose passing days and changing conditions provide a lesson.
rows.anchor: والعصر: الدهر، عن ابن عباس، والكلبي، وأبي علي

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: They identify al-ʿaṣr as late afternoon, which provides a lesson through the night approaching and day receding.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو العشي، عن الحسن، وقتادة

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: He identifies al-ʿaṣr as night and day.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الليل والنهار، عن ابن كيسان

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: He identifies al-ʿaṣr as the middle prayer, the afternoon prayer.
rows.anchor: وقيل: صلاة العصر، وهي الوسطى، عن مقاتل

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: He identifies al-ʿaṣr as one end of the day.
rows.anchor: وقيل: العصر أحد طرفي النهار، عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: He identifies al-ʿaṣr as the misfortunes of time; the author prefers the first interpretation, time itself.
rows.anchor: وقيل: العصر نوائب الدهر، عن علي. والأول الوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity is in ruin because no loss exceeds deserving lasting punishment; the wording may state an inevitable outcome or loss from wasted deeds and deserved Hell.
rows.anchor: أي: في هلاك؛ لأنه لا خسران أعظم من استحقاق العذاب الدائم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He explains loss as the nullification of deeds and deserving the Fire.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بل هو في خسر من إحباط أعماله، واستحقاقه النار، عن الحسن

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: He explains khusr as ruin or loss.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في خسر أي: في خسران، وقيل: في هلاك، عن الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawāṣaw bi-l-ḥaqq means they urge others to obey and follow the truth, which includes all God commands; another explanation narrows it to the Qur'an or to faith and divine oneness.
rows.anchor: وتواصوا بالحق يعني أمروا غيرهم بالطاعة والحق، وهو جميع ما أمر الله تعالى به

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة
rows.claim: They explain al-ḥaqq as the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الحق القرآن، عن الحسن وقتادة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: He explains al-ḥaqq as faith and God's oneness.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الإيمان والتوحيد، عن مقاتل
